title: El Flaco — Belgrano to the Río de la Plata, the Journey of the Poet of Argentine Rock
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Blood of Núñez — Childhood in Bajo Belgrano

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the house at Arribeños 2853, Núñez
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of January Luis Alberto Spinetta is born into the summer heat of Buenos Aires, into a house of tango on the edge of Bajo Belgrano, two blocks from the River. The father, Luis Santiago, sings tangos on the radio; the uncles set the boy on a chair to sing at family gatherings before he is five. In this narrow house on Arribeños the future is already rehearsing: here Almendra will hold its first rehearsals, and Pescado Rabioso after. The child of the tango-singer is appointed to become the poet of a music that does not yet exist.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Canal 13, the program Escala Musical
stops.campa: At fourteen the boy makes his artistic debut on television, singing on the contest Escala Musical and on the children's program La pandilla One and Two. The tango is behind him now; the transistor radio brings the Beatles across the ocean and something breaks open. At the Instituto and among the boys of the neighborhood he meets Emilio del Guercio and Edelmiro Molinari, the ones who will stand beside him at the beginning. The Argentine adolescent discovers the electric guitar as a foreign tongue he is meant to speak in his own accent.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Colegio San Román, the forming of the band
stops.campa: In the schoolyards of the north of the city, among the boys of the Colegio San Román and the neighborhood, the first band takes shape. Spinetta, Emilio del Guercio, Edelmiro Molinari and Rodolfo García find each other over shared records and a shared hunger. They call it Almendra — almond — after the small hard seed that holds a whole tree. They rehearse in the family house on Arribeños, learning to bend the electric noise of the north toward the melancholy of their own city. Four adolescents rehearse in a bedroom the songs that will reorder a nation's music.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Teatro Coliseo, premiere of Muchacha (ojos de papel)
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of June, at the Teatro Coliseo, a nineteen-year-old steps into the light with a song that will outlive the century. He sings Muchacha (ojos de papel) — girl of paper eyes — and the room goes still. It is a lullaby and a farewell at once, tender past its years. Five months before the record exists, the song is already loose in the city, passing from mouth to mouth. Argentine rock, which had been shouting, learns in one evening that it can also whisper.
stops.quote: Muchacha ojos de papel, / ¿adónde vas? Quédate hasta el alba. / Muchacha pequeños pies, / no corras más, quédate hasta el alba.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Estudios TNT, Moreno 970
stops.campa: From April to September, in the studio on Moreno 970, Almendra records the album that draws the map of everything after. Spinetta draws the cover himself: a clown in a pink shirt, weeping, a toy arrow through his head. When the label loses the drawing, he draws it again identical and says, here is another the same, now lose this one. On the back the songs are named not by title but by symbol — the tear, the eye, the arrow. The poet is already refusing to let his work be handled like merchandise.
suggested_refs: Almendra album cover with clown and arrow (1969)

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Plegaria para un niño dormido
stops.campa: Among the songs of the first album he sets down Plegaria para un niño dormido — prayer for a sleeping child — a lullaby heavy with the fear of a world unfit for the innocent it cradles. He is nineteen and already writing as a father writes, already carrying the tenderness and the dread that will run through his whole work. The prayer is not to any god named in a church; it is the poet's own vow to keep watch over the sleeping and the small. Argentine rock discovers that it may pray.
stops.quote: Plegaria para un niño dormido, / quizás tenga flores en su ombligo.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — release of Almendra, RCA
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of November RCA releases Almendra. It is not one thing: folk-rock and psychedelia, string arrangements and the anguish of a boy who has read too much and loved too hard. Alongside Muchacha stand Plegaria para un niño dormido and Ana no duerme — songs that treat pop music as a place fit for grief and prayer. The record is received as the founding stone of a national rock, and the four boys from Belgrano become, overnight, the measure by which the rest will be judged.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the Astral farewell to Almendra
stops.campa: Almendra plays its farewell shows and lets its founder go. The double album Almendra II is already sprawling toward experiment, too large for a single band to hold. Spinetta gives away the finished, adored thing the way a serpent gives away a skin. The crowd that loved Muchacha would keep him singing it forever; he will not be kept. The pattern of his whole life sets here: arrive at perfection, and immediately walk past it toward the unfinished. He leaves the almond to become the rabid fish.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the dissolution of Almendra
stops.campa: As 1970 turns to 1971, after the double album Almendra II, the band comes fully apart. The four are too young and too different; each carries a whole world he wants to make alone. Spinetta, barely twenty, has already given his country its first perfect songs and cannot bear to repeat himself. He walks out of his own legend to begin again from nothing. The gesture will become his signature: to burn the finished house and build another, always toward the un-made thing.

segments.name: The Debt and the Crossing — Europe, 1971

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the thirty-hour session for Spinettalandia
stops.campa: Before he can leave, RCA holds him to one last album on his contract. In February, in a single stretch of thirty straight hours in the studio, half in open war with the label, he records the strange experimental record that becomes Spinettalandia y sus amigos. It is a document of a young man tearing loose from an industry that wants to own him. When the tape stops he is free. The road to Europe opens; the poet pays his debt in exhaustion and walks out the door.

stops.name: Departure — the crossing to Europe
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of March he departs Buenos Aires — Brazil first, then the United States, then Europe — for seven months, with two companions and no band. He walks the streets of a Paris still ringing with May '68, reads Rimbaud in the language Rimbaud wrote, drinks from Foucault and from Artaud's madness. He is nineteen when he leaves as a star and twenty-one when he returns as something stranger: a reader who has decided that rock in Spanish can carry the whole weight of European poetry. The exile is voluntary, and it is a schooling.

stops.name: Paris — the reading of Artaud and Rimbaud
stops.campa: In Paris he finds the books that will remake him. He reads Antonin Artaud — the poet the asylums could not cure, the man of the Theatre of Cruelty, Van Gogh the man suicided by society — and something in the raving French sentences answers a thing in him. He reads Rimbaud's demand to make oneself a seer through the derangement of the senses. He carries these voices home in his luggage like contraband. Two years later they will detonate on an Argentine stage under the name of Artaud.
suggested_refs: Antonin Artaud, Van Gogh le suicidé de la société

segments.name: Pescado Rabioso — The Rabid Fish and the Descent into Artaud

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the forming of Pescado Rabioso
stops.campa: Home again, he forms Pescado Rabioso — the rabid fish — the loudest, hardest thing he has yet made. Osvaldo Frascino, Black Amaya, Carlos Cutaia gather around him; the volume rises, the guitar turns cruel and electric. After the tenderness of Almendra this is the shadow side, the descent. The gentle boy who sang of paper eyes now wants distortion and fury, wants to test how much weight the song can bear before it breaks. Desatormentándonos, the first record, is the sound of a man un-tormenting himself by making more noise than the torment.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the recording of Artaud
stops.campa: The band has already fallen apart, but Spinetta keeps the name Pescado Rabioso for a record that is his alone. He records Artaud — dedicated to the mad French poet, conceived as a reaction against him and toward him at once. His brother Gustavo drums; the old Almendra companions Emilio del Guercio and Rodolfo García return. The songs come acoustic and enormous: Cementerio Club, Bajan, the nine-minute Cantata de puentes amarillos, the two-minute hymn Todas las hojas son del viento — all the leaves belong to the wind. It will be called, again and again, the greatest record of the language.
stops.quote: Todas las hojas son del viento, / ya que él las mueve hasta en la muerte; / todas las hojas son del viento / menos la luz del sol.
stops.quote_source: Pescado Rabioso, "Todas las hojas son del viento," Artaud, 1973
suggested_refs: Artaud LP with irregular octagonal cover, 1973

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Cementerio Club
stops.campa: Within Artaud he builds a song that walks into the graveyard as into a nightclub. The lover, struck dead by tenderness at the mere thought of the beloved, wanders the summer cemetery reckoning the heat there will be without her. Death and desire hold hands and dance. It is the surrealism he brought back from Paris made Argentine, made intimate, made singable — the cruelty of Artaud folded into a melody a boy can play on one guitar in a bedroom. The record refuses every consolation except beauty.
stops.quote: Justo que pensaba en vos, nena, caí muerto. / ¿Quién le dio al pequeño dios el cetro gris del abismo?

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Cantata de puentes amarillos
stops.campa: At the heart of Artaud he raises a nine-minute cathedral: the Cantata de puentes amarillos — cantata of yellow bridges — built from the surrealist current, the cruelty of Artaud, the doomed transgender emperor Heliogabalus, and the burning yellow of Van Gogh's fields. Bridges the color of madness span a river of grief. It is the most ambitious single thing he has yet written, a suite that refuses the three-minute song and dares to be an ordeal of beauty. Here the reader who crossed to Europe pours everything he found back into one long, unbroken breath.
stops.quote: Puentes amarillos, se muere en su jaula... / ¡No! Nunca la abandones.
stops.quote_source: Pescado Rabioso, "Cantata de puentes amarillos," Artaud, 1973

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Teatro Astral, the presentation of Artaud
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of October, at eleven in the morning at the Teatro Astral, he presents Artaud alone — one man, an acoustic guitar, and songs no one has heard. At the door each spectator is handed a printed manifesto: Rock: música dura, la suicidada por la sociedad — hard music, suicided by society — his answer to Artaud's essay on Van Gogh and his rejection of a rock reduced to sex and drugs and empty promiscuity. A fan in the tenth row secretly records the tape. It becomes a golden page in the history of the country's rock, one of only two shows he gives there.
stops.quote: El rock es una música dura, la suicidada por la sociedad.
stops.quote_source: Spinetta, manifesto "Rock: música dura, la suicidada por la sociedad," Teatro Astral, October 1973

segments.name: Invisible — The Trio That Names the College

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the forming of Invisible
stops.campa: He gathers a trio and names it Invisible — Machi Rufino on bass, Pomo Lorenzo on drums, himself on guitar and voice. The name is a wager: that the most important things move unseen, that the essential is invisible to the eye. Out of this trio he will draw his subtlest music, neither the tenderness of Almendra nor the fury of Pescado but a third thing — supple, jazz-touched, tango-shadowed, patient. The band that bears the name of the invisible becomes, itself, a hidden college where three players teach each other what cannot be said aloud.
sources: Wikipedia — El jardín de los presentes

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Durazno sangrando
stops.campa: The second album, Durazno sangrando — bleeding peach — turns inward and eastward. The lyrics rise out of Carl Jung and the ancient Chinese book The Secret of the Golden Flower, a Taoist manual of meditation. A peach falls too early from the tree, its skin the rose-gold of the sun, and splits, and bleeds beneath the water. It is an alchemy of the self set to progressive rock: the ripening and wounding of a soul told through fruit. Here Spinetta is most nearly a mystic, reading the psyche as a garden that must sometimes bleed to open.
stops.quote: Temprano el durazno del árbol cayó, / su piel era rosa dorada del sol.
suggested_refs: The Secret of the Golden Flower

stops.name: Buenos Aires — El jardín de los presentes
stops.campa: The third and last Invisible record, El jardín de los presentes — the garden of the present ones — returns to song and lets the tango he was born inside come back up through the music. The young jazz guitarist Tomás Gubitsch, only eighteen, raises the band to a new fineness even as his presence strains it toward breaking. On this record stands Perdonado (niño condenado) and the tango-rock that closes his most Argentine chapter. He makes it under a military shadow gathering over the country, singing of gardens while the disappearances begin.
suggested_refs: El jardín de los presentes LP, 1976
sources: Wikipedia — El jardín de los presentes
es.paperblog — El Jardín de los presentes

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the dissolution of Invisible
stops.campa: In 1977 Invisible dissolves, worn through by its own tensions, in a country now ruled by terror. The trio that carried his subtlest work goes quiet. Spinetta later says the whole experience frustrated him — not only the band but rock itself, in a nation where playing could cost your life. Yet the name endures beyond the music: Invisible, the college of the unseen, a wager that what matters most cannot be looked at directly. He folds the band away and does the only thing left to a poet under a dictatorship — he keeps writing.
sources: Wikipedia — El jardín de los presentes

segments.name: The Solo Masterworks — A Reader Among His Instruments

stops.name: Buenos Aires — A 18' del sol
stops.campa: Under his own name he releases A 18' del sol — eighteen minutes from the sun — a jazz-inflected record made in the darkest year of the dictatorship. He is reading everywhere now: Foucault on power and madness, Castaneda on the sorcerer's ways of knowing, Rimbaud the seer. Out of these he assembles a private cosmology that he will spend his life setting to music. He is not a rock star performing rebellion; he is a poet-philosopher who happens to hold an electric guitar, building rooms of sound in which a besieged country can still breathe.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Spinetta Jade, the years of the sophisticated band
stops.campa: Across the early eighties he leads Spinetta Jade, a band of virtuosos who fuse rock with jazz-fusion at the highest polish. As the dictatorship falters and then falls, his music turns intricate, harmonically dense, almost weightless. He is now the acknowledged master, the elder at thirty, the one every younger musician measures against. Alfa Beta, Los niños que escriben en el cielo, Bajo Belgrano — the childhood barrio returns as an album title. The exile's son has become the country's musical conscience, and he wears it lightly, always reaching past what he has already solved.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Kamikaze, the acoustic testament
stops.campa: In 1982 he makes Kamikaze, a stripped acoustic record that the critics of the day fail to understand and that time will crown among his greatest. On it stands Barro tal vez — perhaps mud — a song he wrote at fourteen and buried for two decades, and the hymn Seguir viviendo sin tu amor, to go on living without your love. The kamikaze is the artist who dives without hope of return, who spends himself utterly on the song. In the year of the Malvinas war and the dictatorship's collapse, he offers not slogans but the bare human voice.
stops.quote: Y si acaso no brillara el sol / y quedara yo atrapado aquí, / no vería la razón de seguir viviendo sin tu amor.
stops.quote_source: Luis Alberto Spinetta, "Seguir viviendo sin tu amor," Kamikaze, 1982

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Privé and Rezo por vos
stops.campa: In 1986 comes Privé, and on it Rezo por vos — I pray for you — the song he writes with Charly García, the two great rivals of Argentine rock briefly of one mind. The record is electric, saturated, restless, of its decade and against it. He is a man who will not settle into a style, who treats each album as a fresh hypothesis about what music can be. Around him the country is learning democracy again; he keeps doing what he has always done — reading, writing, refusing to repeat the last true thing he found.
suggested_refs: Rezo por vos with Charly García

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Téster de violencia
stops.campa: After two years of silence he returns with Téster de violencia, his most conceptual record in a long while — a dense, brooding meditation named for a machine that measures violence in a body. Here the reader of Foucault and Artaud is fully present: the album takes the wounded modern self as its subject and turns it over in the light. It is not made to please and it does not; it is made to be true. He has become the artist his country most reveres and least understands, and he prefers it that way — the poet always one book ahead of his audience.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Pelusón of milk, the father at home
stops.campa: Married to Patricia Salazar, he fathers four children — Dante, Catarina, Valentino, Vera — and the household becomes a wellspring of songs. He writes Seguí corriendo and the tender Pelusón of milk for them; fatherhood, present since the sleeping-child prayer of his teens, now floods the work. He remains the reader in his study, but the study opens onto a house full of children. The severe experimenter of Téster de violencia is also the gentlest of fathers, and the two are one man, both feeding the same unending song.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Los Socios del Desierto, the return to the trio
stops.campa: In the mid-nineties he forms Los Socios del Desierto — the partners of the desert — a raw power trio, guitar bass and drums, the leanest sound of his life. Decades after Pescado Rabioso he goes back to fury on purpose, sanding the music down to muscle and noise. The elder statesman refuses to become a monument; he wants the danger of the trio again, the risk of only three players with nowhere to hide. Estado de coma and the double album that bears the band's name prove the old rabid fish still has teeth.
suggested_refs: Los Socios del Desierto double album, 1997

segments.name: Las Bandas Eternas — The Five-Hour Summing

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Estadio Vélez Sarsfield, Las Bandas Eternas
stops.campa: On the fourth of December, at the stadium of Vélez Sarsfield, Spinetta gives the concert that gathers his whole life into one night. From twenty forty until half past three in the morning — near six hours, fifty-two songs, more than thirty musicians — he reassembles the eternal bands: Almendra reunited, Pescado Rabioso, Invisible, Spinetta Jade, Los Socios del Desierto. Charly García, Fito Páez, Gustavo Cerati, Ricardo Mollo come up to stand beside him. Forty years of the country's music condense into a single vigil. No one yet knows it is a farewell, and everyone somehow feels that it is.
suggested_refs: Spinetta y las Bandas Eternas boxset (3 CD / 3 DVD)
sources: es.wikipedia — Spinetta y las Bandas Eternas

stops.name: Rosario — Teatro El Círculo, the poet on the pampa's river
stops.campa: In these last touring years he carries the eternal repertoire up the Paraná to Rosario, the river-city that birthed Fito Páez and Che Guevara, and plays the ornate Teatro El Círculo. The country he made a music for now hears him as a living monument, and still he plays as a searcher, not a relic. Age and illness are gathering, unseen, but on stage he is weightless. The wandering bird crosses his own nation one more time, laying the songs down in each city like stones marking a road already almost walked.
suggested_refs: Spinetta at Teatro El Círculo, Rosario
sources: lacapital.com.ar — Spinetta y su rock de autor en Rosario

stops.name: Santiago de Chile — Teatro Nescafé de las Artes, the last concert
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of June he plays what will be his final concert, at the Teatro Nescafé de las Artes in Santiago de Chile, seated through the whole show because of a savage pain in his back. The pain is not yet named; within weeks it will be. He does not know this is the last stage he will stand upon, and so he plays it as he has played all the others — completely, without holding back. The wandering bird comes to rest in a foreign city, and gives, one final time, everything it carried.
suggested_refs: Spinetta at Teatro Nescafé de las Artes, Santiago, June 2011

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the open letter announcing the illness
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of December, to still the rumors, he publishes an open letter through the accounts of his children Catarina and Dante. He writes that since July he has known he carries lung cancer, and that he is well, in full treatment, moving toward a definitive cure. The whole country reads it at once. The man who spent his life refusing to explain his songs now explains, plainly and gently, the one thing he cannot outwrite. The poet faces the last fact directly, with the same clear voice he gave to paper eyes and bleeding peaches.
suggested_refs: the Twitter accounts of Catarina and Dante Spinetta

stops.name: Buenos Aires — CEMIC, Saavedra, the last days
stops.campa: On the eighth of February, after an operation in early January and weeks interned at the CEMIC in Saavedra, Luis Alberto Spinetta dies, aged sixty-two. Buenos Aires goes into mourning: radios play nothing but his songs, crowds gather, a generation grieves as for a father. His son Dante speaks for the family — my old man is music, is light; his body could go no further, but his mind and his soul are shining. The tango-singer's boy, who made rock into poetry in Spanish, passes, they say, to a better plane.
stops.quote: Mi viejo es música, es luz. Y ahora pasó a un mejor plano.
stops.quote_source: Dante Spinetta, on the death of his father, February 2012
suggested_refs: front pages of Argentine newspapers, 8-9 February 2012
sources: excelsior.com.mx — cenizas al Río de la Plata

stops.name: Río de la Plata — the scattering of the ashes
stops.campa: A week after his death his children carry his ashes to the Río de la Plata and give them to the water — the wide brown river that borders the Belgrano of his childhood, two blocks from the house where the tango-boy first sang. He returns to the river that shaped the city that shaped him. All the leaves belong to the wind, he sang; now he belongs to the water. The wandering bird, the poet of the invisible, dissolves into the estuary and is carried out toward the sea, into the country's memory, past the reach of any hand.
stops.quote: Todas las hojas son del viento.
stops.quote_source: Pescado Rabioso, "Todas las hojas son del viento," Artaud, 1973
